svg.title: DDIA 7 · TRANSACTIONS: sketchnote
svg.text: A transaction groups reads and writes into one unit: all of it happens or none of
it does, and concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work.
Postgres defaults to Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB
Tx 2 acted on data that never existed
Read committed: Tx 2 sees the OLD value until Tx 1 commits
Read committed prevents dirty reads (readers see the last
committed value) and dirty writes (row locks until commit). It
Snapshot isolation: Alice's whole tx reads the snapshot from its start → 500 + 500
Snapshot isolation: each transaction sees a consistent
Fix 2: SELECT … FOR UPDATE (lock the row)
Optimistic (CAS): a version column; if 0 rows are updated,
retry. Good under low contention. Postgres Repeatable Read
also auto-detects lost updates and aborts.
rule: at least 1 doctor on call
Same shape: two users book the last room
Fix: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the rows checked · or SERIALIZABLE
Fixes: lock the rows you checked; use SERIALIZABLE; add a
unique constraint; or materialize the conflict by creating a row
per seat or room-night so there is something to lock.
SSI: everyone runs on snapshots without blocking. At commit,
the DB checks whether anything you read has since changed
and, if so, aborts you. Fast at low contention.
"Two users book the last room at the same time."
Write skew. Use a row per room-night + conditional UPDATE, or SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a unique constraint on
Not row locks. Use atomic INCR in Redis, sharded counters, or batch into the DB asynchronously.
Low contention: optimistic version check. High contention on few rows (hot seat map): pessimistic lock or a queue to
No distributed ACID. Use a saga with compensations plus the outbox pattern (Ch 9 and 12).
Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.
